questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Paris has always been a city of dreams for me — not only because of its undeniable beauty and cultural richness, but also because it is the cradle of the French language. As a student of French at Københavns Universitet, immersing myself in everyday life in Paris was the best way to deepen my linguistic skills and cultural understanding.
I was drawn to the academic prestige of Sorbonne Université, known for its strong humanities faculty, and the opportunity to study French in its natural habitat — cafés, bouquinistes, ballet studios, and buzzing classrooms.
Beyond academics, I was inspired by the city’s rhythm — the art, fashion, and café culture — all of which shaped my experience both inside and outside the classroom.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was quite difficult to find the information I needed. Sorbonne’s website was very outdated and confusing to navigate, especially when trying to access course listings and timetables. Important details were often missing or scattered across different platforms. I had to rely on other exchange students and forums to piece together essential information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received minimal assistance upon arrival. There was, though, a formal orientation or welcome event for international students – but in French, and very short. Most of the administrative help came through email correspondence, which was often delayed or unclear. It took a long time to get clarity on course selection, and there was little to no support in helping students settle in.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Despite the administrative struggles, once classes started, the academic experience was rewarding. However, I would strongly recommend Sorbonne to improve its communication and support for international students, especially during the crucial first weeks of arrival.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was fortunate to be accepted into the Fondation Danoise at Cité Internationale Universitaire de Paris during the first round of applications. The process itself wasn’t too complicated, although the waiting time felt a bit nerve-racking. I would highly recommend applying early, as spots fill up quickly. Overall, it was a smooth and manageable experience compared to other housing options in Paris.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living at Cité U — and especially in Fondation Danoise — was an incredible experience. Not only was it likely the most affordable option in Paris, it also offered a vibrant international community and easy access to the city. I always felt safe, and the campus surroundings were beautiful and peaceful. Future students should know that housing in Paris is notoriously expensive and competitive, so applying early (and broadly) is essential. Also, don’t underestimate the value of having other international students around — it made all the difference socially and emotionally.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I’m incredibly grateful for my time at Fondation Danoise. It made my exchange experience feel like home, and I would absolutely recommend it to other Danish students going to Paris.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The registration process was frustrating and old-fashioned. Many courses, especially those in French, required physical registration on paper, and even small changes had to be done in person during short and inconvenient office hours. For English-taught courses, the process was handled through email, which was slightly better but still inconsistent and slow. Overall, the system felt outdated and not designed with international students in mind.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Most French courses had to be registered for manually by visiting the administration office and requesting your paper file, which you would physically update if you added, changed, or dropped a class. This made things unnecessarily complicated and time-consuming. For English courses, it was handled through email, but responses were often delayed or unclear. There was no central online portal where you could manage your choices or see your complete schedule.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: One aspect I really appreciated was the support I received for my mental health. I disclosed that I had a psychiatric condition, and the university was very understanding. I was granted accommodations, such as extended exam time, shorter written assignments, and the freedom to leave the classroom during exams if needed. This made a big difference for me and allowed me to focus more on learning rather than managing stress.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I didn’t end up getting any of the classes I originally planned to take, which felt disappointing at first. But in hindsight, it turned out to be a blessing — there were so many incredible courses to choose from, and the ones I eventually got were absolutely perfect for me. They challenged me, inspired me, and I ended up doing really well academically. I truly wouldn’t change a thing.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be prepared for last-minute changes and expect a certain level of disorganisation — but don’t panic. Things might not go according to your plan, but that doesn’t mean they won’t work out beautifully. Stay flexible, ask other exchange students for advice, and trust that you’ll end up in classes that suit you, even if they weren’t your first choice.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic programme surprised me in the best way. Though the path was winding, the destination was exactly where I needed to be.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took BA-level courses during my exchange, and overall, the academic level felt more demanding than what I was used to at UCPH. The structure was more rigid, and there was a greater emphasis on individual study and memorisation. However, as an international student with a documented disability, I was met with great understanding. My professors were incredibly kind and accommodating, which helped balance out the intensity of the academic expectations.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: To be honest, the teaching style at Sorbonne wasn’t all that different from what I’m used to at UCPH. It was a mix of lectures and some student interaction, depending on the professor. The main difference was the structure around registration and course management — not the actual teaching. I also really appreciated how understanding and flexible my professors were when it came to my disabilities. They made sure I felt comfortable and supported, which created a safe and encouraging learning environment.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would highly recommend the course Études théâtrales – Contemporary British Drama: Ethics and Aesthetics. As someone who is very creative, I found it incredibly inspiring — the discussions were rich, and it gave me a lot of freedom to interpret and express ideas.
I also really appreciated the distance-learning course in French. It was well-structured and gave me the flexibility to manage my own time and workload, which was especially helpful during stressful weeks. Both courses challenged me in the best way and helped me grow academically and personally.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had to visit both a doctor and a hospital during my stay, and unfortunately, I had to pay for everything out of pocket. My private insurance didn’t cover it, and the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) was of no help at all in my case. It came as quite a shock, especially since I had expected most healthcare to be covered. I recommend other students look very carefully into their insurance coverage before going abroad — especially when it comes to specialist visits and emergencies.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Surprisingly, groceries were less expensive than I had expected — especially the basics I needed for simple meals. I was able to find affordable options at local supermarkets like Franprix, Carrefour, and Monoprix. That really helped me keep my daily costs down. On the other hand, cafés and eating out could be quite pricey, so I mostly stuck to cooking at home or grabbing coffee and small snacks instead of full meals.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Skip the packed museums and the long tourist lines — the real magic of Paris is in the streets. I recommend simply getting lost in the city. Walk for hours with no destination. Let yourself wander into hidden courtyards, small boulangeries, and charming squares. Sit down at a café, order a coffee or a noisette, and strike up a conversation with someone nearby. The soul of Paris reveals itself slowly, in moments of spontaneity and softness. Trust it — and trust yourself.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Paris is magical, but it can also be intimidating at first. People might seem distant, and the bureaucracy can be overwhelming. But once I found my rhythm — my walking routes, my favorite café, my safe places — I adjusted beautifully. The key is to observe, adapt, and embrace the small rituals of daily Parisian life. It didn’t take long before it truly felt like home.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: French students can seem reserved, but they’re often warm and curious once you break the ice. I recommend joining specific seminars or smaller classes where it’s easier to talk. Don’t be afraid to ask for help or offer to study together — it’s a great way to connect. Also, showing genuine interest in French culture (even if you make mistakes!) always goes a long way.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The administrative system was the biggest cultural shock — it was slow, confusing, and deeply paper-based. I also found that personal space and direct communication were handled differently than in Denmark. But with time, I learned to navigate it all with patience, a bit of charm, and a deep breath. It taught me resilience in a very French way.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I truly appreciated how open and friendly people actually were — despite the stereotypes, I found it easy to start conversations, especially at cafés. The café culture itself was something I fell in love with: sitting for hours with one drink, watching life pass by, and connecting with strangers who often became friends. There’s also a romantic quietness to how Parisians go about their day — slow mornings, beauty in small details, and a deep respect for art, language, and presence.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don’t trust the stereotype — Parisians are actually very kind if you approach them openly and speak a bit of French.
	2.	Be prepared for a chaotic registration process and old-school administration — stay patient and flexible.
	3.	Explore everything outside the classroom: take walks, talk to strangers, sit at cafés, and let the city shape you.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
If you plan to take extracurriculars like ballet or sports, be aware that the cultural tone can be very different. I took ballet classes in Paris and the teacher was quite harsh and body-focused — something that’s still considered normal in traditional French ballet culture. It was challenging, but also eye-opening.
Also: bring copies of every single document you might need — printed, signed, and in multiple versions. It sounds silly until you’re standing in a Sorbonne hallway begging someone to accept your form…

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Finding out that I could build a life from scratch — in a new city, a new system, with a new rhythm. I formed friendships with strangers, walked miles through Paris every day, learned how to survive chaotic bureaucracy, and still managed to thrive. I grew more confident, more independent, and more in love with the world. The quiet moments — a solo coffee, a successful conversation in French, a walk in the golden light — were the most rewarding of all.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Navigating the French bureaucracy and the disorganised university system was incredibly frustrating at times. From course registration to medical care, I often felt like I was left to figure things out alone. It tested my patience and resilience. But I also struggled with maintaining mental health in a high-pressure environment far from home. Fortunately, I reached out and found support — and that made all the difference.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
Paris wasn’t always easy, but it was unforgettable. I left with more than just academic credits — I left with stories, lessons, friendships, and a stronger sense of self. I’d do it all again in a heartbeat.
And to anyone going: say yes more often. Speak French even when you’re scared. Wear what makes you feel beautiful. Walk everywhere. Sit in the sun. Live it slowly.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
